results.title: Alert Triage via Drift-Adaptive Exploration for Human-in-the-Loop Anti-Money Laundering
results.abstract: Anti-money-laundering monitoring divides work between a model and a team of analysts: the model ranks transactions, analysts review as many alerts as their capacity allows, and the labels they return are the model’s only supervision. A budget spent on the highest-scoring alerts maximizes immediate seizures while leaving the model blind to patterns it has not yet learned. This exploitation-exploration trade-off is known in fraud detection, but how to adapt the split of a review budget to concept drift has received little attention. We propose DAT, a drift-adaptive triage policy that splits the review budget between a detection and an exploration channel. It selects the highest-risk transactions for detection, then transactions that are uncertain under the current model or distributionally novel for exploration, clustering the latter so the budget buys distinct information rather than near-duplicates, and adapts the split online from two drift signals: the analyst hit rate in the detection channel and the divergence between the current and the training distributions. Every alert carries the reason it was raised so that a team can tell a seizure case from a learning case, a design element we specify but do not evaluate, because our analysts are simulated. Replaying the labeled Elliptic Bitcoin transactions step by step with simulated analysts at a 10% budget and a 1-step label delay, DAT retains 52% of its pre-shift illicit-class F1 after the documented distribution shift, against 42% for a drift-triggered policy that widens exploration only once a detector fires and 36% for pure exploitation, while catching as many illicit transactions as either, 707 against 692 and 680, and at no measurable cost in pre-shift F1. The review budget is an enforcement resource and a learning channel at once, and DAT lets a team set how it is divided.

results.title: Who Really Decides in Large Language Model-Mediated Triage? The Placement of Decision Authority Across the Human-AI Workflow
results.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly involved in health-related interactions in which their outputs may influence clinical judgment and action, yet existing validation approaches do not fully capture how decision authority is distributed across the human–AI workflow. We conceptualize decision-authority placement (DAP) as a configuration-level, safety-critical construct linking workflow, intended use, and validation in LLM-mediated triage, and specify its four constitutive, assessable dimensions. Unlike classifications of decision authority at the deployment level, DAP assesses whether practical authority enacted in use corresponds to, or diverges from, its intended placement. Grounded in established accounts of how authority is organized in interaction, and informed by a focused illustrative overview of intended-use validation, human–AI decision support, automation, decision-authority concepts, and LLM triage-adjacent evaluations, DAP comprises four constitutive dimensions: output status, task-specific user competence, delegated decision function, and action closure. These dimensions specify how practical authority over triage-relevant functions is assigned, constrained, or displaced across human–LLM interaction and workflow. Comparative application across three plausible triage configurations shows that similar LLM functions can have different safety implications depending on where authority is placed. Accuracy and output-performance remain necessary, but their safety meaning depends on the configuration in which LLM outputs are interpreted and translated into action. Validation should therefore move beyond model outputs alone and assess the human–LLM configuration through which decision authority is enacted across users, tasks, and care pathways.

results.title: Unvalidated Trust: Cross-Stage Vulnerabilities in Large Language Model Architectures
results.abstract: As Large Language Models are increasingly integrated into complex automated pipelines, security vulnerabilities that extend beyond simple input filtering become a practical concern. This work presents a mechanism-centered taxonomy of 41 recurring risk patterns, identified through a standardized, text-only evaluation protocol on commercial LLMs under default settings. Our empirical observations reveal systemic weaknesses in unvalidated trust inheritance across processing stages, which allows inferred intent to propagate without adequate verification. We find that inputs are frequently interpreted non-neutrally, leading to implementation-shaped responses or unintended state changes even in the absence of explicit commands. These behaviors constitute architectural failure modes in which internal interpretation and state management create opportunities for compromise. We therefore recommend adopting zero-trust architectural principles, including provenance enforcement, context sealing, and plan revalidation, to mitigate these cross-stage vulnerabilities. As motivation for this approach, we introduce Countermind, a conceptual blueprint for implementing such defenses.

results.title: Reducing Under-Triage Risk in Large Language Model Based Clinical Triage Using UMLS-CUI Augmentation
results.abstract: Abstract Background Public facing large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health guidance, including triage recommendations. We evaluated whether augmenting LLM prompts with standardized clinical concepts from the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) could improve the safety and robustness of clinical triage recommendations. Methods We used a publicly available dataset comprising 60 clinician-authored clinical vignettes, each represented in 16 demographic and narrative variations, yielding 960 vignette-factor combinations. Clinical entities were extracted using a two-stage pipeline combining ClinicalBERT-based named entity recognition with rule-based identification of laboratory abnormalities. Extracted entities were mapped to UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs).Negated concepts were excluded. A confidence-weighted CUI voting classifier was trained using empirical associations between CUIs and clinician-assigned triage categories. We compared five approaches: CUI-only classification, MedGemma 27B, MedGemma 27B augmented with CUIs, GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-4o-mini augmented with CUIs. Outcomes included overall accuracy, under-triage, over-triage, emergency-case accuracy, and sensitivity to anchoring statements. Results CUI augmentation decreased under-triage but increased over-triage in both models tested (GPT-4o-mini and MedGemma 27B). It improved high-acuity recognition while reducing recognition of low-acuity cases. CUI augmentation had mixed effects on overall triage accuracy; accuracy increased for MedGemma 27B but decreased for GPT-4o-mini. Emergency-case accuracy improved from 73.0% to 80.7% for GPT-4o-mini and from 60.5% to 68.5% for MedGemma 27B. CUI augmentation also reduced susceptibility to anchoring statements. These findings suggest that the principal value of CUI augmentation may be shifting model behavior toward safety-oriented behavior rather than uniformly improving overall accuracy. Conclusions Ontology-grounded prompt augmentation shifted LLM triage recommendations toward greater sensitivity to high-acuity presentations and reduced overall under-triage. These safety gains were accompanied by increased over-triage and mixed effects on overall accuracy. A hybrid architecture combining LLM-based language understanding with interpretable UMLS-derived clinical concepts may improve the safety and robustness of AI-assisted triage. Further evaluation using real-world patient communications and clinical outcomes is warranted.

results.title: Simulation-Derived Human Triage Data Improve Lightweight Large Language Model Performance in Mass-Casualty and Tactical Triage: A Multi-Dataset Prompting Study (Preprint)
results.abstract: BACKGROUND Mass-casualty and operational triage require rapid decisions under uncertainty, yet real-world labeled decision data from these settings are scarce, heterogeneous, and difficult to collect at scale. Immersive virtual reality (VR) simulation provides a controlled way to generate structured human triage data in realistic high-consequence scenarios. OBJECTIVE To evaluate whether simulation-derived human triage examples improve the performance and safety profile of a lightweight open-weight large language model (LLM) beyond zero-shot prompting and explicit triage guidance alone, and whether the pattern is observed in simulation datasets organized around Sort, Assess, Life-Saving Interventions, Treatment/Transport (SALT) and Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC). METHODS We performed a retrospective computational evaluation using structured cases derived from immersive VR triage simulations. Four prompting conditions were evaluated: zero-shot, context/guideline only, simulation-derived few-shot examples only, and few-shot examples plus context. In the TCCC-oriented analysis, few-shot examples were evaluated from both a matched TCCC-derived source and a cross-source SALT-derived source mapped to the four TCCC labels. Outcomes included accuracy; F1 score, which balances precision and recall, summarized as macro-F1 and weighted-F1; per-category F1; under-triage; critical under-triage; pooled failure modes; attribute-stratified performance; few-shot sensitivity; and prompt-elicited model confidence. TCCC row-level evaluations contain repeated presentations and are interpreted descriptively. RESULTS For SALT, test accuracy was 68.2% with zero-shot prompting, 68.4% with context alone, 71.1% with few-shot examples, and 79.1% with few-shot plus context; macro-F1 was 51.7%, 57.2%, 70.7%, and 83.8%, respectively. In TCCC, few-shot-plus-context accuracy was 87.0% with matched-source examples and 88.1% with cross-source examples; the corresponding context-only accuracies were 68.6% and 70.9%. The gain from adding examples beyond context alone was 10.7 percentage points for SALT, 18.5 points for matched-source TCCC, and 17.2 points for cross-source TCCC (pooled descriptive gain, 17.8 points). Category-level results showed large gains for EXPECTANT with simulation examples, while SALT DELAYED remained the weakest category. SALT critical under-triage decreased from 11.1% with few-shot prompting to 0.4% with few-shot plus context. TCCC under-triage decreased from 9.8% to 5.5% in the matched-source analysis and from 9.8% to 4.9% in the cross-source analysis; critical under-triage was 0% in both few-shot-plus-context source conditions. Prompt-elicited confidence remained high even when predictions were wrong and did not provide a reliable case-level safety filter. CONCLUSIONS Simulation-derived human examples improved lightweight LLM triage performance beyond explicit framework guidance alone. The effect was observed with both matched-source TCCC examples and cross-source SALT-derived examples, and the strongest conditions reduced safety-relevant under-triage. These findings support immersive simulation as a practical source of reusable human decision data that preserve observed variation and experiential judgments not necessarily encoded in written guidance or reproduced by model-generated synthetic cases, with potential relevance to other high-consequence domains where real-world decision data are scarce. TCCC estimates are descriptive because many rows are repeated presentations of a much smaller number of patient identities, and the results do not establish readiness for autonomous or real-time clinical triage.

results.title: Human in the Loop Might Not Be Enough: Large Language Model Oversight in Pediatrics
Cross-Model Variability in Large Language Model Triage Behavior for Potential Stroke Symptoms
results.abstract: Abstract Background Stroke is a time-sensitive neurological emergency in which early EMS activation and presentation to definitive care are cornerstones of effective therapy. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted by the public for medical advice, but the veracity of the guidance provided by commercially available models responding to potential stroke symptoms is not well understood. Methods We performed a cross-model benchmarking study comparing the triage choices of three frontier LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, and Llama 3.3-70b-versatile) on first-person vignettes describing a unilateral arm symptom on waking, across 10 symptom descriptors, and two clinical phases (before and after a partially reassuring self-examination), with or without a clinical distractor (n=50 per condition). Results Claude sought emergency care most often, Llama least, and GPT-4o in between, diverging most sharply in the post-examination phase where Claude called 911 in 100% of runs, Llama called for non-emergency help in 100%, and GPT-4o was symptom-dependent. A distractor shifted behavior away from emergency care in almost all conditions: calling 911 fell from 37.9% to 14.6% and waiting rose from 0% to 45.9% in the post-examination vignette. Responses were also sensitive to symptom word: weak, limp, heavy, and clumsy generated higher alarm, whereas numb, tingly, odd, strange, and weird generated less urgent responses. Conclusions The increasing use of LLMs for medical advice has significant public health implications. Commercially available LLMs show significant model-to-model variability and framing sensitivity when confronted with potential stroke symptoms, including under-recognition of canonical CDC warning descriptors, underscoring the need for systematic benchmarking as these tools become de facto first points of contact for patients experiencing neurological emergencies.

results.title: Effect of Prompt Structure on Large Language Model-Recommended Triage Levels in Urologic Patient Messages
results.abstract: Abstract Purpose. To evaluate whether prompt structure changes large language model-recommended triage in urologic patient messages and whether safety-focused prompting reduces unsafe undertriage without increasing overtriage. Methods. In this scenario-based, cross-sectional, comparative study, 50 synthetic urologic patient messages were tested in three prompt arms: a neutral base prompt (P1), a red-flag-focused prompt (P2), and a safety- and triage-calibration-focused prompt (P3). This yielded 150 first-response outputs in Turkish from GPT-5.4 Thinking. For each case, two urologists predefined the gold-standard triage level and required core warnings. Primary outcomes were complete concordance, unsafe undertriage, and overtriage; omission of critical warnings was secondary. Results. Complete concordance was 45/50 (90.0%) in P1, 42/50 (84.0%) in P2, and 41/50 (82.0%) in P3. No unsafe undertriage or omission of critical warnings occurred in any arm. Overtriage was 2/50 (4.0%) in P1, 8/50 (16.0%) in P2, and 9/50 (18.0%) in P3. Compared with P1, overtriage was significantly higher in P2 and P3 (p = 0.031 and p = 0.016, respectively), with no difference between P2 and P3. Conclusion. In this dataset, safety-focused prompting did not improve unsafe undertriage but increased overtriage. Evaluations of patient-facing artificial intelligence should therefore assess not only red-flag recognition but also whether the recommended level of care is appropriate.
